top_choice_rationale: Optical lattice clocks rest on a distinct, demonstrated idea: the magic-wavelength condition equalises the dynamic polarisabilities of the clock states so that thousands of atoms are held in a Lamb-Dicke lattice without a leading-order light shift. This moved both stability and accuracy to about 1e-18, and independent laboratories have reproduced and surpassed it. The two-name allocation (Katori for the concept and first demonstration, Ye for the accuracy and stability frontier) has no arbitrary exclusion, and a citation confined to magic-wavelength lattice trapping avoids reading as a repeat of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. The quantum spin Hall trio (P002) is the strongest rival on conceptual reach but has a harder Mele-or-Hasan and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang attribution; magic-angle graphene (P003) is less mature, with the mechanism open and first-author experimentalists uncredited; no award ranks last because a mature, well-attributed candidate exists.
recusal_note: No connection to Katori or Ye documented in profile; documented ties to L'Huillier, the Lund attosecond groups, Keller's ETH group and Lindgren's Gothenburg group do not involve any proposed laureate. Disclosed field affinity: polarisability and blackbody-shift theory is adjacent to lattice-clock physics; no recusal need apparent.
